papers.title: Chaotic-Periodic Alternation in a Financial System with Double Delays
papers.abstract: In this paper we present the chaotic-periodic alternation phenomenon within a three-dimensional nonlinear financial system subjected to Pyragas-type time-delayed feedback, as well as the lag effect of the interest rate in the price index dynamics. Through numerical analysis, transitions to chaos, including period-doubling cascades, period-halving routes, and incommensurable-period dynamics are characterized. The emergence of chaotic-periodic alternation are found and described. Results suggest that minor timing misalignments in the inner dynamics of a financial system, as well as those considered in the feedback loop can induce systemic volatility.

papers.title: Chaos without Local Spectral Instability in a Kicked Oscillator
papers.abstract: A damped harmonic oscillator kicked by a pulsed periodic potential can be chaotic although every local Jacobian has eigenvalues inside the unit circle. Damped rotation between kicks lets non-normal shears of opposite curvature compound, so ordered products of contracting Jacobians amplify perturbations. We derive the exact joint spectral radius of the Jacobian family and an exact Lyapunov-exponent decomposition showing how this geometric pumping overcomes dissipation. The proposed mechanism can be realized with laser-cooled trapped ions in a pulsed optical lattice.

papers.title: Basin Adjacency Graphs: A New Approach to Characterizing Basins of Attraction
papers.abstract: Fractal basins of attraction are commonly characterized through resolution-dependent measurements, such as box-counting methods, uncertainty exponents, and basin entropy. Here we introduce a different approach based on the adjacency relations between connected components of the basins, without retaining their detailed spatial geometry. A finite-resolution basin diagram is represented by a graph with one vertex per connected component and edges linking adjacent components belonging to different basins. We investigate how the number of vertices scales with the spatial resolution $N$, following a power law $N^\alpha$ in the systems considered. Under suitable assumptions, the exponent $\alpha$ is related to the Kor\v{c}\'ak exponent of the component-size distribution and can coincide with the box-counting dimension of the basin boundary when its fractal structure arises from the proliferation of components. The graph also provides adjacency-based diagnostics that may help characterize basin configurations exhibiting the Wada property. We illustrate the approach using idealized Sierpi\'nski constructions, the Newton and relaxed Newton families, and three dynamical systems with previously established Wada basins.

papers.title: Directed Wada cascade in systems with discrete scale invariance
papers.abstract: Dissipative systems whose equations are unchanged by a dilation can host an infinite ladder of attractors, each shell an exact magnified copy of the one before. Since such dynamics cannot tell a magnification from its inverse, the natural expectation is that these basins are maximally entangled, with every boundary point lying on the boundary of all of them, following the Wada property. We find that this expectation fails, and fails in a precise way. Dilation covariance and a single trapping region together bound which basin boundaries a point can lie on, and the bound depends only on its distance to the origin. No point lies on the boundary of all of them. The basins on whose boundary a point does lie are the deeper ones, as we prove for the stable manifolds of the boundary saddles and support numerically for the rest of the boundary, so the boundaries nest in one direction only. We call this structure a directed Wada cascade, and the standard Wada tests, as usually applied, do not detect it. It arises in maps whose nonlinearity is a log-periodic modulation of a homogeneous function, because the same periodicity builds the ladder through mode locking and confines the orbits. We show the cascade in maps that differ in invertibility, nonlinearity, scaling exponent and dimension, and in a flow.

papers.title: Tendex Lines and Short-Time Deformation: The Geometry of Lunar Tides
papers.abstract: Tendex lines and the stretchlines and squeezelines of Lagrangian coherent structure theory share a geometric construction: they integrate eigenvector fields of symmetric tensors. We connect their dynamical interpretations through the short-time deformation of particles released with zero initial velocity relative to a freely falling reference in an autonomous gravitational field. The leading departure of the Cauchy--Green tensor from the identity is quadratic in time and equals the tidal tensor multiplied by the squared observation time. The tidal tensorlines therefore give the limiting principal stretching and squeezing directions. For the planar lunar field, these tensorlines are radial lines and concentric circles centered on the Moon. The same tidal tensor defines a Lorentzian metric whose null directions have no quadratic change in line-element length. Its null geodesics are logarithmic spirals, describing the short-time limit of finite-time unit-stretch geometry. Near Earth, the principal tensorlines clarify the two outward tidal tendencies, while the null directions distinguish vanishing leading extension from vanishing relative acceleration.

papers.title: Stochastic-layer width as an order parameter for the integrability-to-chaos transition in the bouncer model
papers.abstract: The transition from integrable to chaotic dynamics in the conservative bouncer model is investigated within the phenomenological framework of continuous phase transitions. In the integrable limit, $\epsilon = 0$, the action variable is conserved and the phase space is completely foliated by horizontal invariant curves. Introducing a weak periodic perturbation, $\epsilon > 0$, destroys resonant tori and generates localized stochastic layers around the fixed points of the mapping, even at parameter values where global phase-space portraits appear predominantly regular. By dividing the angular domain into discrete bins and extracting the extreme action values visited by a single chaotic trajectory, the upper and lower boundary curves of the stochastic layers surrounding the period-one fixed points $(\pi, 0)$ and $(\pi, \pi)$ are reconstructed numerically. For the fixed point $(\pi, 0)$, the stochastic layer develops in the region $V \geq 0$ and is bounded by two curves, whereas around $(\pi, \pi)$ the layer extends across both sides of the line $V = \pi$ and requires a four-boundary characterization. In both cases, the mean width of the stochastic layer acts as a geometrical order parameter that vanishes continuously as $\epsilon \to 0$ and obeys a power-law scaling proportional to $\epsilon^{\alpha}$, with exponents $\alpha = 0.496 \pm 0.001$ around $(\pi, 0)$ and $\alpha = 0.496 \pm 0.006$ around $(\pi, \pi)$. The associated response function diverges in the integrable limit, providing clear numerical evidence of critical behavior belonging to the $\alpha \simeq 1/2$ universality class of weakly perturbed Hamiltonian systems.

papers.title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
papers.abstract: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.
